speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, July 4, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mac-Fachen for the second reading of Bill No. C-207, to authorize the making of contributions by Canada toward the cost of programs for the provision of assistance and welfare services to and in respect of persons in need.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. E. Pascoe (Moose Jaw-Lake Centre):
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose last night I was commenting about repeated statements of previous speakers from our party regarding the need to provide our senior citizens with higher old age pensions to offset at least partially the effects of the ever increasing cost of living.

I stated that in moving for a $100 a month old age security pension the members of the Progressive Conservative party are not advocating something new to that party. An old age security pension of $100 a month was a plank in our platform during the 1965 election campaign. I referred to this campaign commitment during meetings with senior citizens of my riding, and that is why I now speak on their behalf.
Last night I stated that it should be the duty of each of us in this house to express his or her views on the need for higher pensions for senior citizens who are trying to live on the present old age security payment of $75 per month. The hon. member for Waterloo North agreed that our senior citizens are entitled to fair treatment, and stated specifically last night that pensions provided at this time under the Old Age Security Act are insufficient.
The hon. member for Brantford stated that he had been advocating changes in the Old Age Security Act for the benefit of senior citizens without the requirement of a means test, and I should like to quote his exact words as they are recorded at page 7095 of Hansard for June 30. He was referring to previous speakers when he said:
I believe the debate indicated that they had a feeling which is shared all over this house that the means test or even the needs test, which is an improvement over the means test, should not be used with regard to the senior citizens of Canada.
I am sure many other members on the government side would express the same opinion if they should take advantage of the opportunity of speaking during this debate. I heard the hon. member for Essex South express views along this line during a radio interview, and perhaps he will put these same views on Hansard.
The records in Hansard to date show clearly that we in the Progressive Conservative party have been pressing for a $100 a month pension since this session commenced on January 18. The records also show that the Liberals with Social Credit support have consistently voted against any pension increase. I mention these facts to emphasize the concern of the members of this party for our senior citizens. We believe they should be treated in a more fair manner. Members of the N.D.P. have attempted to take credit for what we in this party have tried to do in respect of this matter, but this party's record in this regard will stand comparison with the record of any other party.
July 5, 1966

Let me point out that the record of the former C.C.F. government of Saskatchewan does not indicate that that party was above criticism in its treatment of senior citizens. I recall hearing complaints about a strict means test being applied before supplementary payments to old age pensioners were allowed, and those payments in many cases only amounted to a niggardly $2 per month. I am sorry the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam is not in the house at this time to hear these remarks, because he was the leader of that party and the premier of Saskatchewan at that time.
I am speaking in support of a pension increase because I promised to do so in replies I made to many senior citizens in my riding who have written me personal letters or forwarded petitions regarding an increase. I could have brought a whole sheaf of petitions from my file, but I have only brought one or two which I intend to use as examples.
The petition I have in my hand is from the National Pensioners and Senior Citizens Federation and is written over the name of Mr. Nathan W. Medd, president, who lives in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan. I shall not read the resolution, but I wish to point out that the National Pensioners and Senior Citizens Federation reaffirmed their request that the federal government increase the old age security pension to $100 per month.
I know personally many of the people who have written about pension increases as well as many of those who have signed petitions, and I know their needs. I am sure the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Health and Welfare have received similar letters and petitions because I have received copies of some that were sent to those gentlemen. Surely I need not point out to the Prime Minister or the Minister of National Health and Welfare that public opinion has been aroused regarding the need for more consideration for those individuals who helped build our country but who have now passed the income earning stage.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
There are reports that the minister will announce some form of income increase to those in their later years who can prove need. It will be interesting to learn just how far our demands of the past few days have induced the government to alter or add to the legislation before us. I join with other speakers in protesting against what the government wishes to call a needs test but which is actually only another name for a means test.
Canada Assistance Plan Under such a system, as the hon. member for Queens commented, not only must one be poor but one must prove to some official of the state that one is poor.
I have here a petition from the National Pensioners and Senior Citizens Federation which contains the comment: "By changing the word 'means' to 'need' is just eyewash." I have another petition from the Senior Women's Committee for Pension Increase which says: "Senior citizens and families won't tolerate humiliating needs test."
If the government is not moving to increase the old age pension to $100, for which we are pressing, we hope that the means test or the needs test will be removed from Bill C-207. It will be interesting to hear from the Minister of National Health and Welfare in this regard.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to take up much of the time of the house on this matter. However, there are two points I should like to bring to the minister's attention which I do not think have been brought to his attention so far in this debate. Before I do so, however, I should like to reiterate the plea made by most members on this side of the house that the minister persuade his colleagues to reconsider this question and provide $100 a month without a means test to the old people of this country who will not benefit under the Canada Pension Plan right away.
The other two items I wish to bring to the minister's attention are these. When regulations are made in connection with this legislation after it eventually passes the house, I hope that particular attention will be paid to the section referring to disabled persons and the disabled persons allowance. This matter has been raised by me many times in the house and by hon. members in various parties, particularly the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Smith). I refer to the existing regulations with respect to the disabled persons allowance.
At the present time a person wishing to receive the disabled persons allowance practically has to have both arms and both legs off. This works a great hardship on many people. I am sure every hon. member in the house has dealt with this problem many times. I suggest to the minister again, and I hope this time he pays some attention to my suggestion, that he persuade his colleagues that employability should be the criterion whether a person should receive the disabled persons

July 5, 1966
Canada Assistance Plan allowance. If people are so disabled and ill that they cannot work for a period of time, let us say six months, they should receive the disabled persons allowance for as long as they are unable to work. If at some time in the future they are able to work, of course the allowance should be discontinued.
At the present time the regulations require that a person be totally and permanently disabled to receive the allowance. Most doctors, probably because they think they will never be in this shape themselves, will not sign a certificate saying that a person is permanently disabled if there is one chance in a million of his getting better. This regulation has worked great hardship on all kinds of people in this country. I hope the government will see that it is changed when the new regulations are promulgated under the act or arrangements are made with the provinces.
The last item I bring to the minister's attention is the question of mothers allowance. Under this legislation the federal government proposes to help pay mothers allowance. I hope that when this measure comes into effect the minister will make certain that some of the regulations that exist in some parts of Canada in this regard are removed. The fact is that if a husband deserts his wife and children the mothers allowance cannot be paid, no matter how much it may be needed by the family, as long as the husband can be found within a certain period of time. If the husband disappears permanently and cannot be found, the wife receives the mothers allowance in respect of her children, but if the husband turns up just once in Timbuktu or somewhere else and is found for just one day the allowance is cut off no matter how practically impossible it is for the mother to receive any assistance from such husband. This is a ridiculous situation. I hope that the minister, when arrangements are made with the provinces or regulations are drawn up under this legislation, will see that this iniquitous situation no longer exists.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of extending the debate and I am not responsible for its extension until this afternoon, because I had made up my mind not to practise any obstruction against the government regarding the legislation now before us and entitled "Canada Assistance Plan."
The fact remains, nevertheless, that so many things have been said and so many stands

have been taken that I can hardly allow the debate to end without saying a few words to explain my position. At the beginning of the session, when the opposition introduced a non-confidence motion against the government with regard to a $100 increase in the monthly pension, I then voted with the government, because 1 realized it was merely a non-confidence motion which, had it been passed by the house, would probably not have settled the problem of older people. It would simply have embarrassed the government perhaps to the extent of bringing about another election. But at any rate, it would have delayed the passage of this social assistance measure promised by the present government at the time. Along with many others I waited with some anxiety to study the provisions of the bill to be introduced and designed to help needy Canadians.
We now have before us this piece of legislation under the form of Bill No. C-207. I am not suggesting that this bill is perfect, because I know of no party and of no government which have ever passed perfect bills in this house, but I say it is nevertheless a noteworthy effort of good will in spite of the inadequacies of the bill. Following this lengthy discussion which has lasted at least a week, and thanks to the numerous suggestions constructive or otherwise, which have been made, the government will certainly be able to improve this piece of legislation.
I, for one, am satisfied, Mr. Speaker, to see that the government respects the constitutional authority of provinces in the field of assistance to the needy, since it intends to support the provinces in the proportions mentioned in the bill. This is quite satisfactory.
I am satisfied to see that the government not only wishes to help the aged, our senior citizens, the old folks, those who are no longer young, but that it also wants, according to the bill, to help those who are in need in all areas, the unemployed, the disabled, the widows, the needy of all kinds.
I think that those who have been saying for a week that there is nothing in the bill, nothing good, that the bill means nothing, are not being fair. We must understand, Mr. Speaker, that this bill, even though it is not perfect, offers something; it is certainly an improvement on what existed before, and we should at least, instead of dragging on the debate interminably, all say together: Well, let us give that at least to the needy for the time being; let us give it to them as soon as possible, and afterwards, we shall consider improving the situation, which is not perfect.
July 5, 1966

It is sure that if we accepted the suggestion to give immediately $100 a month to the elderly people this would not settle the problem, because there are many elderly people who need more than $100. This bill provides for some medical care, some related aid which would mean to them more than $100 a month. At any rate, is it really fair to give $100 to those who do not need it and then refuse $125, $130 to those in need? We should wonder about that.
The point that we should consider, Mr. Speaker, and about which the opposition has better justification, is the objection to a needs test. Experience proves that these tests are usually made by incompetent persons, who lack tactfulness and the necessary circumspection; they often take the form of an inquisition, which is humiliating for the needy, who have a legitimate self-respect, and in many cases have to go through certain methods of inquiry which are vexatious and unacceptable.
* (3:40 p.m.)
The main recommendation, I believe, that should be made to the government about this bill is that those who are called upon to come into contact with the needy, the elderly people, widows, unemployed, etc., should follow training courses to learn tactfulness and warmth which should characterize all the actions of social service workers, which is charity or philanthropy in certain cases, but which, in the present case, is a service due to all taxpayers.
A great number of these taxpayers have already paid taxes on considerable amounts to guarantee the efficient application of such acts to the needy, and they are entitled to be treated with due respect. I should like to stress that point Mr. Speaker, and in this respect I endorse the criticism of the opposition. The methods of investigation should certainly be improved upon, as should the methods of all who are in contact with the needy in order to eliminate red tape, police investigations, receipts and all kinds of things that add to the hardship of those unfortunates for whom life has not been overly generous.
Now the fact remains, at least in my province, that the program will be administered by the province. If my province were to decide to pay $100 per month to the elderly persons, to the old people, I cannot see what objection the federal government would have; if my province were to decide to pay $125 per month, I do not believe the federal government would object. So I say that the bill,
Canada Assistance Plan although it may not seem as generous as the members of the opposition, or most of them, claim, it is opening the door in a generous way.
It was urged since the beginning of the debate that the act should be made to apply uniformly, Mr. Speaker. I hardly think the needy can be taken care of in a uniform manner in Canada, because the needs are not the same. At this point I repeat what I said a while ago: to give $100 or $150 to an elderly person who does not need it is too much; yet giving $125 to a senior citizen who needs $150' is too little.
The opposition, Mr. Speaker, claimed that it was not resorting to what the Americans call a filibuster. The claim was made sometimes with a tongue-in-the-cheek attitude. Sitting in this far corner as an independent, Mr. Speaker, the impression I get is that several members have taken the opportunity of this debate for some electioneering, and that is the impression that is gathered here. All sides of the house claimed not to be playing politics, I think. But I feel there has been too much politicking going on, while the contrary was being claimed, at the expense of the old people and of the needy. I do not think this is proper. I do not say that to blame all those who took part in the debate, but simply because I have enough respect for my colleagues to know that they are all aware of their responsibilities toward the Canadian people and particularly toward this least favoured class of Canadians. I say that to appeal precisely to their conscience as Canadians. Even if they have temporarily stilled it to satisfy certain electoral interests, the debate nevertheless should not be prolonged in this tone; on the contrary,we should remember that the poor are waiting for a bill.
The present bill may not be perfect, but it nevertheless represents something. Even if it is not perfect, let us pass it as soon as possible and try to pass others to remedy the situation within as short a time as possible. We will pass other bills sooner if we do not prolong debates in the house indefinitely.
Mr. Speaker, it is easy to use subjects such as this one to criticize the government. It is always easy, as a member of the opposition and as an independent member, to tell the government that it does not do enough: $100 is not enough, $125 is not enough. As an independent member I know that I will have nothing to administer tomorrow and no responsibility with regard to the national

I think too many did that; but I believe there are many left who were aware *of the needs of the poor and I think the government would be wise to hear the demands of those who made objective, positive and realistic representations.
Let us say to ourselves, for the time being, Mr. Speaker, and I believe it is the fairest way to put it-and you must admit I listened to everybody before rising to speak-that the bill as introduced by the government is a very elaborate one, representing a considerable improvement, compared with the present situation.

The government must remember that in the final analysis the stumbling block of all those measures intended to assist the underprivileged, the needy, is the manner in which the bounties of the nation are distributed among them, the way investigations are made; those are the things that should certainly be improved, humanized and made less vexatious.

This enthusiastic support of the legislation took place at a time when the principle of tjbe bill and the provisions of
Canada Assistance Plan the bill were being considered on their inherent value by hon. gentlemen opposite. This attitude continued until the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) intervened with an amendment which was ruled out of order and about which I shall say more in the course of my remarks.
The hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Rynard) described the Canada Assistance Plan in the following words:	"The plan
before us is a good plan." The hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Winkler) stated that this proposal is a reasonably wise one and the sooner it is put into operation the better because it will be of benefit to the recipients. The hon. member for Portage-Neepawa (Mr. Enns), whose words in this debate have more significance than those of any other hon. member because of his experience in this particular field, made this statement:
-as a statement of intent, this resolution will commend itself readily to members of the house and all Canadians. . . . This measure can be an exciting, revolutionary step, perhaps the most revolutionary among the whole group of public welfare acts . . . The Canada Assistance Plan, if utilized responsibly and generously across Canada, will mean a long stride toward goals which welfare agencies have coveted for Canadian families.
The hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) says that this measure is an attempt to fill the gaps that have been left by existing plans. The hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Brand) states:
I sincerely hope . . . that the idea will be to provide rehabilitation if at all possible as the prime concern of this proposed plan, because I think it is so much more important to human dignity to give people the opportunity to fend for themselves and to provide for themselves.
Finally, the hon. member for Saint-Hyacin-the-Bagot (Mr. Ricard) described it as a brilliant statement of intentions. Even in the pre-amendment phase, the pre-political phase of this debate, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre told the house that it was most encouraging to learn there had been a wide measure of federal-provincial co-operation, which was very much to be commended, and that the federal government was prepared to share financially in a number of programs in which to this point there had been no federal-provincial participation. He said that when we weld together these programs and have federal-provincial co-operation, federal-provincial participation, the better it will be for all concerned. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre stated, "I welcome that progress .

July 5. 1966
Canada Assistance Plan
This measure might well draw these comments from hon. members opposite in the pre-amendment phase of the debate because the measure, on its merits and because of its provisions, deserves separate treatment and separate decision of the house. The Canada Assistance Plan, as has already been stated, will provide a basis for co-ordinating all public assistance programs in Canada. It will, over a period of time, replace existing categorical programs and enable federal and provincial governments to provide assistance to needy persons regardless of the cause of need. The plan will provide federal sharing for the first time in mothers' allowance programs covering 200,000 needy mothers with dependent children, and make it possible for these mothers and their children to receive assistance on the basis of need and on the basis of the family budget. Hardly a word was said in the debate with respect to this aspect of the Canada Assistance Plan.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
The plan will provide federal support for the strengthening of the administration of, and the welfare services related to, social assistance programs. If the plan did not have the capacity to improve administration and to provide proper and qualified welfare services, then some of the comments made by members opposite would have validity.
The plan provides for federal aid for buttressing child and youth welfare agencies. For example, in the field of child and youth services, 50,000 children in the care of child welfare authorities in Canada will receive assistance under this plan.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, all the recipients of public assistance will for the first time have their health care costs met on this basis. There is no federal ceiling on the benefits under the new program, and the federal government stands ready to share with the provinces, on the basis of need, not only in the new categories or new groups which I have already mentioned but also in the improvement of the level of benefits now being paid to the recipients of old age assistance numbering 85,000, the blind numbering 8,000 and the disabled numbering 55,000.
Several hon. gentlemen opposite referred to the severe medical tests under the disability act. Through the Canada Assistance Plan any person who is disabled for any reason by disablement of any kind and to any extent will be able to be assisted without having to meet the severity of the medical test which has been so widely condemned by hon. members opposite.

The new cost to the federal treasury in this year will be $85 million. The total federal outlays in this fiscal year, 1966-67, will be $250 million and the total commitment by federal and provincial governments will be $500 million, affecting one million people who are to be covered under this program. In terms of the size of the expenditure involved and from the number of Canadians to be assisted, this program is to be a very substantial program indeed.
It has been suggested that the Canada Assistance Plan is only a tidying-up operation. It is true, as the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith) pointed out, that it will bring together existing programs, we hope and give them a comprehensive foundation. But it is more than that. It attempts successfully to deal with the causes and effects of poverty.
The hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Rynard) pointed out the necessity for breaking the dependency cycle of families who, from one generation to another, are dependent on public welfare. You can dish out, Mr. Speaker, as much money as you like but this in itself will not break the dependency cycle; more than that is needed. The recipients of public assistance must be given a real chance to get off welfare, to break the dependency cycle, and because the Canada Assistance Plan lays the foundation to do this it is an important milestone in the history of public welfare in Canada.
The preventive and rehabilitative aspect of the Canada Assistance Plan is its positive aspect, and this has hardly been mentioned in this debate which has gone on for so many days. Hardly a mention has been made of the welfare services that will be available to recipients of public assistance, including counselling and training of various kinds, to help to solve these difficult personal problems that keep people on welfare.
Hardly a mention has been made of the work activity projects that will be supported under this plan, giving the opportunity to disadvantaged persons to resume gainful em-orientation, or to those who are handicapped ployment on the labour market through re-to be able to do something to become part of the productive population in Canada.
There has been hardly a mention in this long debate of the possibility under the Canada Assistance Plan of reaching agreements with the provinces by which the Indian population of Canada will be given an opportunity, in so far as welfare is concerned, to be treated as other Canadian citizens.

A typical situation arises from the use of budget standards normally set out in provincial regulations based on budget studies. These studies indicate amounts necessary for
Canada Assistance Plan the various items of food, clothing, hospital supplies and personal needs of people who require assistance. The amounts in those tables are generally schedules derived from budget studies, a method which the hon. member for York South described yesterday as being sensible. Additional amounts can be and have been paid to cover such important variables as shelter, fuel, utilities and special needs.

I want to say to the Minister of National Health and Welfare that even though he was waxing eloquent in his rhetorical flight he should not have distorted what I said about the needs test. I said it clearly on two occasions. I said that the needs test is an improvement on the means test. I said I was glad to see that where we now have means testing we are making the forward step of moving to needs testing. When I made very clear my approval of the needs test as better than a means test where there is now a means test, it did not mean that I approve of a needs test being established where there is not now a test of any kind. My complaint with regard to Bill C-207, and it is right here in clause 2 of the bill now before us, is that a needs test is being introduced for persons in the old age security bracket. These people are having a needs test put on where they now do not have a means test or any test whatsoever. It is about this that we complain. It is against this that most of the speeches on this side in the last few days have been directed.
I remind the Minister of National Health and Welfare that when I spoke the second time on this question I asked him to be fair and not to misquote what I said on a previous occasion. But he chose to misquote it and interpret my approval of a needs test as better than a means test as meaning that I accept a needs test any place at all. I say again so that anyone other than the minister, I am sure, can understand it, that where we now have a means test it is good to have an improvement and have the needs test put in its place. But it is still a retrograde step, for which this parliament should hang its head in

July 5, 1966
Canada Assistance Plan shame, that in the terms of clause 2 of this bill we are introducing a test in an area where we now do not have one.
The parliament of Canada in 1951 took one of the most advanced steps it has ever taken in the field of social legislation by passing an act that removed the means test for persons 70 years of age and over. Only a few months ago the parliament of Canada extended this progressive step by making provision for the means test to be removed year by year right down to the age of 65. It was a good step when we took it in 1951. It was a good step when we took it last year. But what the minister is asking parliament to do now is to take the retrograde step of putting a needs test in where there is no test of any kind at the present time.
My statement, the statements of my colleagues and the statements of members in other parties that this is a retrograde step, that this is an affront to the dignity of our senior citizens, is one that stands up in light of the speech the minister has made. He has invited us to argue this point and I hope we can yet persuade him that whatever the parliament of Canada proposes to do for our older people should be done without a means test or a needs test of any kind.
Clause 2, as I say, covers all the various definitions including that of need, and it includes the word "age", making it clear that at the moment this is what the government of Canada is proposing to do for our aged people, namely, give them only the benefits that are in this bill. Therefore it seemed to me that it was not only appropriate for members of the House of Commons to argue that something better should be done for our senior citizens than was provided in this legislation, but I think it was appropriate for the minister to tell us on several occasions that if we would just let the debate on second reading end he would respond to those suggestions and tell us what the government was going to do for senior citizens. Not only did he tell us that in the house, not only was this his answer and the Prime Minister's answer when we asked for a statement on motions, but in ways this government has the information was leaked out that if only the debate on second reading would come to an end the minister would make a statement telling us the government's intentions with respect to the recipients of old age security.

information at the present time. I submit that the Minister of National Health and Welfare misled the house and misled the country by telling us that this statement was going to be made when he concluded the debate on second reading and then standing up this afternoon and refusing to make that statement.

He knows it will not stand up to what the Canadian people expect.

I see the name "endocrinology" and I suppose it is the medical term in connection with endocrine glands, etc. A reading of the bill shows that it is a fairly extensive measure. I presume this society will have a membership that is provincial, federal and international. The schedule of the bill indicates that a number of companies are involved. This is why I would like the hon. member to explain the bill. The schedule indicates that such places as Australia, Argentina, Belgium, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Czechoslovakia, Denmark, Ecuador, Germany, England, Haiti, Holland and Hungary are involved. The schedule enumerates on two and a half pages societies that are already formed. The interesting thing is that the head office of the international society will be situated in Canada in the city of Montreal.
It is unfortunate that the sponsor of this bill is not here, because I presume the purposes of the bill will bring credit to Canada in that the head office of the society is being established in the city of Montreal. The society will itself determine the type of bylaws it will have in effect. It is interesting to note that, unlike some other bills with which the house deals, there is written into this bill a clause that in my opinion is very worth while and should commend itself to sponsors of other bills. A reading of the bill shows that clause 4 is concerned with the head office of the society, which it says shall be in the city of Montreal, in the province of Quebec, or at such other place in Canada as the society may determine by bylaw from time to time. Then there is this subclause added:
Notice in writing shall be given to the Secretary of State by the society of any change of location of the head office, and such notice shall be published forthwith in the Canada Gazette.
This is a very interesting provision and I believe it is something the committee should recommend for future bills, because in the choosing of a head office we have found that a number of companies have had to come before parliament and have new legislation

enacted to enable them to change their address. This has been achieved by means of a very cumbersome piece of machinery whereas a very simple appendage to the statement of the location of the head office, which would allow any company to change the address of the head office by applying to the Secretary of State and publishing the change forthwith in the Canada Gazette, would achieve the desired purpose in a much more simple way.
I believe this is a very worth-while provision and it should recommend itself to the members of the committee who are interested in taking out of parliament many of the bills that are nothing but a nuisance when companies have to come before us to change the number on the board of directors or make other changes. If a clause were written into the original act it would allow changes to be made in the number of directors, where the head office will be, where the annual meetings will be held and so on. This method of dealing with the problem would get rid of the difficulty that has existed in changing the name of a company. Also, there has been a major problem in respect of some companies in putting into the French language the title of the company. This has been a difficulty in the past because the titles of some companies are not easy to translate into the French language.
It is interesting to note that the International Society of Endocrinology is in French translated into La Societe Internationale d'Endocrinologie, and I suppose our French members would agree that this is a simple, straightforward translation of the English name. The way I pronounced it would not really convey that impression. The functions of the society are not clearly dealt with in the bill. The society has asked for power to develop a constitution and make bylaws, rules and regulations as long as they are not contrary to this act. I presume the bill has been carefully studied by lawyers versed in international and constitutional law who are in a position to assess whether the bylaws of this international agency would be acceptable to the many countries already involved in that they have branches of this society.
I note that some countries, including England, have two such societies. Mr. Chairman, the Bank of Western Canada has been a fairly controversial bank. The bill to incorporate it has had a rough passage not only in the house but in the committee as well. If hon. members are interested in the amendments, they may look at Votes and Proceedings No. 41 for Tuesday, March 15, and they will see that there are six or seven pages of amendments to this bill. I am sure the sponsor of the bill would like to say a few words on the amendments that have been moved as well as the problem raised by the fact that some questions have

July 5, 1966

been asked about whether or not there are dummy directors for the company.
One of the directors is the former president of the Bank of Canada who apparently has a very small number of shares but has played a fairly large role in the development of the Bank of Western Canada. Apparently this bank is not in fact, a bank of western Canada at all. It is an additional bank which will be situated in the city of Winnipeg but the financial control will remain in the city of Toronto. There was some discussion of this situation in the committee, and whether or not members were satisfied with the explanations I am not able to say.
This was a simple bill of only three pages but now there are four pages of amendments which I believe raises a problem. I would be remiss in my duty if I did not mention these facts. In my opinion the move to establish the Bank of Western Canada and the Bank of British Columbia should have been taken into consideration after the discussion of the amendments to the Bank Act. At that time consideration could have been given whether or not this bank was going to perform the usual functions of a bank.
It is true that the banking industry in Canada is not under monopoly control, but from the point of view of the borrower and the depositor the banks in Canada are really a monopoly operated in conjunction with the state bank, the Bank of Canada. For this reason there has to be a certain amount of consideration given to any banking legislation because it is obvious that banks play an important role in our country. They are important for the loans they make and for the facilities they provide. They are important too in their relations to the Bank of Canada, which is an establishment that can be used for the good of the nation.
I am therefore very sympathetic to the idea that people in western Canada will have the opportunity of having a bank of their own. I regret the fact that it has been necessary to look at the sponsorship of this bill, and I am not referring to the parliamentary sponsorship. I refer to the provisional directors of the company. One who is not named seems to have a great deal more influence behind the scenes in connection with this bank than the person who has been named chairman of the board of directors, I presume pro tem, Mr. Coyne.
We are well aware of the fact that there are parts of western Canada that have not been served sis well as they could be by

existing banks. For this reason it was not surprising that the other chartered banks in Canada did not in any way oppose this measure. There are a limited number of chartered banks, I believe only 11, of which six provide the majority of the banking service for most Canadians. The fact that these banks did not oppose this measure indicates they were not prepared to provide the service themselves in many of the areas in which the sponsors of this bill indicated they were prepared to provide service. For this reason the Bank of Western Canada possibly will serve a useful purpose.
I am hopeful that the day will come when not only the Bank Act will be changed so there will be a better opportunity to assess the banking needs of Canada but there will also be an opportunity to see what the policies of some segments of the banking system may be. It is a fact that you can go to one bank in a community with a certain proposition, outline this proposition to the bank manager and indicate what your collateral is, and if you are turned down at that bank and walk across the street to another bank you will be turned down in exactly the same way. In my opinion there is absolutely-I underline "absolutely"-no competition whatever between banks. I suggest that the Bank of Western Canada is going to be no better and no worse than the other banks.
I believe we should not be passing this bill but that we should be introducing a national banking authority to bring all the banks under some central control. It is interesting to note that while we talk about a 6 per cent interest rate for the banks there are indications that is not always the rate. I presume this bank will adhere to the same policy the other banks have. Someone says that the law provides the banks can only charge a 6 per cent interest rate. This is not true. Every one of the banks has a different interest rate for various types of loans. They have an interest rate that includes the 6 per cent, plus insurance and a number of other charges.
I was in a bank and we were discussing the rates of interest on small loans. I mentioned the rate of one bank and the manager said: That is not the rate over there; it is so much. He pulled a form from his desk drawer and showed me the rate on small loans at the other bank. It was interesting to note that the bank interest on small loans was running anywhere from 6 per cent to 8 per cent. The manager was quite willing to show me how they arrived at these charges.

It is interesting to recall that a few years ago the Imperial Bank of Commerce appeared before the banking committee and was willing to testify it had a bank rate considerably higher than 6 per cent. The bank was willing to outline how it arrived at this rate. It was interesting also to note how the lawyers got into the question because some of the officers of the Imperial Bank of Commerce were asked how they got away with having various rates of interest. They said they had legal advice which indicated that if they followed a certain pattern they would be able to increase the bank rate for certain loans under given conditions. The other banks indicated at the time that they were not interested in pursuing this course, their legal advisers having indicated it was not legal. It is interesting to note that since that time all the banks have gone into this business so either the lawyers had a change of heart or the banks saw some reason for the change.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
It seems to me we are not taking into consideration the over-all needs of the country and that there is a similarity between these banks and the insurance companies which operate in a monopoly position. It is true that not every Tom, Dick or Harry can start a bank in Canada, although I understand that when my ancestors first came to this country they could and did do so. Whether or not they went broke escapes me, but it certainly has not rubbed off on me and I have not inherited anything from them. Therefore I do not know whether it was a good thing that we allowed at that time a variety of small provincial banks in one community to be owned by one individual.
It is true that in this country the banking industry has weathered the storms which have plagued other countries. I think it is safe to say that for at least the last 20 years no one who has deposited money in a bank has found it less advantageous than depositing it under the mattress at home, and some people may consider it more advantageous and even a little safer.
However, the purpose of this bill, let us face it, is not to provide a service. If we really want to provide a service to the Canadian people we should nationalize all banks and thereby provide the same service to all the people. If such were the case people in Toronto would not find it necessary to say that no money is available for mortgages. In my area the farmers would not complain
Private Bills
about no money being available to buy extra equipment or cattle for the farm. They would not say there was tight money or loose money, and they would be able to obtain money as the Minister of Finance decided money should be made available.
At the present moment a gentleman's agreement exists. The minister says "Let us tighten up the money supply". He said that a short while ago and all the banks played the game. I wonder whether those in the Conservative party who a few years ago did not have much faith in Mr. Coyne would expect him to play the game if he were the chief director of this bank. When he was asked to play the game he might not play the game, though he might be an exception. This sort of thing may be good or it may be bad. The situation here may not be the same as with other banks to which we have granted charters, and therefore we may find we will repent that we granted this company a charter, even though I am sure there are many people in western Canada who are looking forward to having a bank on their street to provide service.
It should be quite clear to the Canadian public by now that banks are not only supplying service. A bank is not just a place to deposit money but also a place which provides wealth to those who deposit a few dollars toward its incorporation. The only consolation I have is that these banks will not get rich on the amount of money I deposit in them, whether they have branches in Ontario or elsewhere. Although there is some advantage to those who incorporate a bank, there is less advantage offered to those using the facilities of the bank.
I suggest that in passing this bill we may open a chink in the banking industry of Canada, particularly with the vindictiveness that Mr. Coyne may feel toward some governments for some time to come. If so, this will bring us much closer to the day when we reach the goal of which I am personally in favour, namely, nationalizing the banking industry of Canada and having one large bank with outlets in every town in the nation to supply credit where credit is needed and on a much more equitable base than I have found in many local offices, particularly when they have to call upon the collector for the next two years. If this is the accomplishment in years to come I will be very happy to lend my small support to the passage of this bill.

Mr. Chairman, as you recall this bill has previous consideration in committee of the whole on April 26 last. It has, of course, been in the parliamentary hopper for quite some time now, along with another proposal to establish what has been referred to as a regional bank, namely, the Bank of British Columbia.
As 1 have said on other occasion when we have had these measures under discussion, I believe that, properly handled, the development of regional banks in a country as widespread as ours and with the diversity of economic interests we have in different regions in Canada, can serve a useful purpose as long as our basic system of banking as we know it now is maintained. At this moment we do not exactly know what the government may have in its mind in regard to the future of the banking system, except in a very general way. We do know that the two banks being proposed will come under the regulations and rules of the new bank Act, whatever form they may take, and in that respect at least they will be in the same category as any other bank in Canada.
As far as I am aware, the other new bank which is being proposed, the Bank of British Columbia is not being organized in the present bill along the lines which were originally proposed. The former bill would have enabled the provincial authorities in British Columbia to direct its policy in the public interest, but I understand it will be a genuinely regional bank.
So far as the Bank of Western Canada is concerned I am not quite so sure in my own mind that it will operate in accordance with the manner in which the name proposed for it would suggest. The question has been raised, and I think quite well documented, that while it is being called the Bank of Western Canada its control is not going to lie among western Canadians. In this connection I would like to refer to remarks made on April 26 by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands as reported at page 4339 of Hansard, in which he said:
We have been told that one of the purposes of organizing this bank was to have a financial institution in western Canada, based in western Canada, owned by people in western Canada and directed by people in western Canada. But what do we find?
He then went on to deal with some of the evidence that was adduced in the committee on banking and finance which made it clear that so far as the financial control of the

equity capital of this bank was concerned this was not actually going to be the case.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
The hon. member concluded his remarks at page 4339 of Hansard. I shall not read everything he said but only his words in conclusion.
Obviously this bank is not only going to be directed by three eminent financiers from Toronto but is going to be owned substantially by residents of central Canada, not of western Canada.
Then he added:
I have no objection to people of central Canada owning property such as this but I do not think they should masquerade as residents of western Canada devoted to the interests of western Canada. This is one of the things that give me some concern.
It is true, Mr. Chairman, that I share the concern expressed by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands. I only hope that some of the attention which has been focused on the discrepancy between the name of the bill and the actual ownership may serve to put the management of this bank on the alert so that they will make a genuine attempt to prove that some of the fears expressed have been unfounded. I hope that if they are going to portray themselves as the Bank of western Canada they will in fact devote their major attention to meeting the needs of western Canada with respect to banking services to an extent that some of the other chartered banks in this country have not done. I hope that they will deliberately shape and form their policies to that end so that the people of western Canada will derive some benefit from the establishment of this bank and the policies which it will follow. The people have not always derived adequate benefits from the other chartered banks which have their headquarters in the eastern part of the country.
I am not making these remarks in any sense of trying to set one region of Canada against another but only with the idea that all regions of Canada should develop economically and so develop the strength of their industry that the strengthening of one region can serve to make Canada as a whole a stronger nation in the economic and financial field. I hope that this will turn out to be the case in respect of the Bank of Western Canada if it finally receives approval and is incorporated under the laws of this parliament.
I note that the hon. member for Timis-kaming made some references to one of the persons who is named in this bill who is

When the committee turned to other matters at six o'clock I was developing the point that the minister had made a commitment in the house to make an announcement concerning assistance to old age pensioners. The references he made on this matter in the house have been placed on record by my hon. friend from Winnipeg South.
I wish to point out that the minister went further. He and his staff were busy convincing newspapermen, the people who cover parliamentary proceedings and sit in the gallery, that he was waiting and that he would have made a statement on Wednesday, or on Thursday, or on Friday-he could scarcely contain himself, and if only the nasty people in this corner, the members of the New Democratic Party who for purely political and party reasons were carrying on a filibuster would cease their activities, he would come forward and announce his proposal.
Not only did he indicate to the press that he was ready to make a statement, but details of that statement were spilled out. I do not know whether the minister saw the press himself or whether it was his very competent executive assistant who did so, or whether it was his public relations advisor, whom I saw sitting just above the press gallery only about five minutes ago.
I wish to place on record a few of the press stories which I suggest were inspired from the minister's office. They appeared in the press across Canada, not only on Wednesday of last week, but since then. I would begin
July 5. 1966

with the Winnipeg Free Press which carried
a story on Friday, July 1, by Victor Mackie. I start with this because I notice Mr. Mackie sitting in the press gallery. It begins:
Costing the federal treasury nearly $300,000,000 a year Health Minister Allan MacEachen is expected to make an announcement soon that the federal government has decided to provide a transitional old age pension benefit. It will likely become effective Jan. 1, 1967.
Later, Mr. Mackie says:
The minister is prepared to make the announcement He wanted to make it Wednesday. But if he made the statement it could close off the filibuster the New Democratic party has launched calling for an increase in the basic old age pension from $75 up to $100 a month and the lowering of the age limit to 65 years.

Political gamesmanship at the expense of the nation's old people continues in the commons today as members enter their fifth day of debate on the Canada Assistance Plan. Several times last night opposition spokesmen refused to grant Health and Welfare Minister MacEachen the floor to make an announcement about increased pensions.

The House of Commons is locked in a sham battle as the politicians compete to win the favour of the nation's needy old age pensioners.

In the third place, I think this legislation will give social workers more scope in preventive and rehabilitative work than they have had heretofore. Instead of having to wait until the families and individuals are in a very bad way they will be
[Mr. Orlikow.l
able to step in at an early stage of distress and difficulty.
The social workers will have much more scope to do preventive work and also to pioneer along new lines of rehabilitation. In the fourth place, I think undoubtedly this legislation will help secure more and more highly trained social workers. This is important in an age like ours where training is very necessary. In the last place, I think it is going to be very valuable because it will include the Indians under the same provisions as other people. I think this is a very essential and long overdue form of restitution which we are making to some of the native people in this country.
I wanted to quote that, because it was said this afternoon that none of us made any reference to the good and necessary features in the bill.
Now I wish to go on to deal very briefly with one or two of the features in this bill which I think are long overdue and very necessary in this country. I know that social workers in certain parts of the country are looking to this legislation as a means of getting ahead with child care, day care, nursery care, or whatever you choose to call it. In Canada we do not know exactly what we have or how much we need in the way of day care. We do know that we need a great deal more than we have at the present time. We know that in 1965 there were 2,020,000 Canadian women working for pay outside of homes. Of these, 1,054,000 were married;
191.000	were widowed or divorced. Sixty per cent of the married, widowed or divorced women-about 757,000-had children under the age of 16.
Who takes care of these children while their mothers are at work? The women's bureau of the Department of Labour in Ottawa did some research on this in eight Canadian cities. They found that most of these women,
757.000	of them, do not pay for the care of their children. They do not pay for it because they cannot afford to pay for it. Instead their children are left with the grandmother, with another adult or, worse still, an older child.
[DOT] (7:20 p.m.)
This is the situation to date in Canada. I was interested to find out how little accurate information on the amount of day care there is available across Canada. I came across a statistical work prepared recently by the Canadian Federation of Business and Professional Women, which indicated a shocking lack of day care services in existence in Canada in relation to the need. British Columbia is one province which is a little better off in this regard than many others, yet in that province there are only 311 institutions of this kind available, including
July 5, 19BS

private nurseries, private kindergartens, kindergartens, co-operative nurseries and day care nurseries. These institutions look after in the neighbourhood of 15,720 children. In addition there are 33 foster day care homes with an enrolment of 192 children. In that province there is provision of this kind for only 15,912 children.
The business and professional women's researcher discovered that in Alberta there was concern on the part of women's groups and family welfare agencies which resulted in the licensing of day nurseries, nursery schools and play schools by the department of public welfare. All facilities in Edmonton, with two exceptions, are privately operated either through a voluntary organization or a private enterprise. The only figures available show that the total number of children provided day care in the city of Calgary is 2,085. Information available in respect of Medicine Hat indicates that some children receive this type of care, but the number is not available.
In the province of Saskatchewan-and the minister will note that that province is under new management-at the present time there is provision for 90 children. In Manitoba no figures are available as to the amount of care provided, but I have learned that there are only four licensed day care nurseries, an unknown number of private nurseries, unlicensed operators and relatives and neighbours who provide this type of service.
In New Brunswick the day care nurseries look after 703 children. When one tries to find information of this kind in respect of Nova Scotia he is reminded of the Iron Curtain, because no information is available. Even the department of public welfare is unable to provide accurate information on the number of children for which day care provision is made. No information is available in respect of Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland or Quebec.
In Ontario information is available only in regard to the city of Toronto and the city of Ottawa. In Toronto some 20,018 children are enrolled in various types of day care schools, and in the city of Ottawa 360 children are enrolled in similar schools.
Admittedly there may be a few more such day care nurseries in operation in Canada than those for which we have figures, but on the basis of our information there are only 39,088 children being looked after through this kind of service. There are approximately
757,000	working mothers; so when you consider that only 39,088 children are being
Canada Assistance Plan provided with day care, you realize how absolutely impossible the situation is and you wonder what happens to the approximately three quarters of a million children who are being left on their own, without any day care provision.
I believe that this bill will do a great deal to help make funds available for the establishment of day care schools, provided provincial governments and local welfare authorities take advantage of this provision. The next hurdle that must be overcome relates to the lack of information about day care in those provinces I mentioned. I suggest that, because no information is available in this regard, this is a clear indication that provincial governments may not use the provisions of this bill to the greatest advantage. I hope they do, because this is a very far-reaching form of service.
Another form of service which may receive assistance through this measure is the homemaker service, and here again this should be regarded as a preventive service. This type of service which will now become available in Canada I am sure will prevent many Canadian homes from being disrupted and broken. I know nothing more conducive to broken homes than mothers going out to work and leaving their small children without proper care. Homemaker service is a very valuable form of service. I do not know the exact amounts of money that will be made available for this type of service during the remainder of this year, but I hope that when the minister replies he will give us some indication.
Let me make a brief reference to another form of service, neighbourhood services. This is a new service being provided in Canada. There are four agencies at this time in Canada that provide this service and they are located, as might be expected, in the four largest cities. In Montreal there is the Association of Neighbourhood Services; in Toronto there is the Association of Neighbourhood Services; in Winnipeg there are the Neighbourhood Service Centres and in Vancouver there is the Association of Neighbourhood Services. These organizations are all affiliated with the Canadian Association of Neighbourhood Services, the Canadian Welfare Council and the National Federation of Settlements and Neighbourhood Centres.
I believe that these organizations will be eligible for funds under this program because their purposes are: first, to stimulate public interest in the role of neighbourhood services

July 5, 1966
Canada Assistance Plan within the total welfare services structure; second, to serve as spokesmen for neighbourhood services on matters of national concern; third, to serve as a medium for the exchange of information and ideas regarding local and international developments in neighbourhood services; fourth, to co-ordinate neighbourhood service projects of national scope; fifth, to foster fact-finding studies and research in neighbourhood services and provide consultative services; sixth, to establish standards of practice for neighbourhood services and seventh, to encourage the development of neighbourhood services in areas not now served.
The Company of Young Canadians expects to place some of its volunteers in positions with neighbourhood services of the nature I have described, for the purpose of assisting the people in underprivileged areas in finding a better and more adequate way of life. They will help these people extricate themselves from the vicious circle of complete dependency on welfare. Some of these people have been dependent entirely on welfare agencies for two or more generations. These programs will assist them to get out of this situation and once more get into the stream of community living. I hope they will be among the agencies which will qualify for grants under this program.
I believe that training of social workers is another area which deserves assistance. While I am referring to this aspect I should like to point out something I forgot to say when I was speaking the other day. One of the biggest arguments for a flat over-all increase in old age pensions under the old age security plan is the relative lack of highly and properly trained social workers. It is a shame to think of taking our few adequately, highly trained social workers and making them spend their time totting up people's incomes and measuring them against a needs test, when these workers are needed for other much more desirable services such as social and rehabilitative work. I think they should be devoting their time to these things, rather than fussing around about means tests, when we have a perfectly good income tax system to take back the surplus from people who do not need it.

In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I wish to say that I believe this legislation offers real hope to welfare people across this country and to provincial welfare departments. If the provinces and the local welfare people will take advantage of it, I think it can be made to

create a real advance in our social work outlook across Canada. This is a measure that is long overdue and that will be welcomed. The fact that it does not do the big job of looking after the older citizens of this country in the way in which that job should be done does not mean that we do not recognize its value in so far as it goes. We thought we had made that clear before. If not, I hope I have made it abundantly clear that' I think this bill has good features and should be welcomed for what it is.

The heart of this legislation, having in mind the things for which it provides, is what is generally referred to as the needs test which it is proposed to establish in place of the means test in various pieces of social welfare legislation. When one looks for the definition of the needs test he has to turn, I would say, first of all to subparagraph (g) of clause 2 which reads as follows:
"person in need" means
(i) a person who, by reason of inability to obtain employment, loss of the principal family provider, illness, disability, age or other cause of any kind acceptable to the provincial authority, is found to be unable (on the basis of a test established by the provincial authority that takes into account that person's budgetary requirements and the income and resources available to him to meet such requirements) to provide adequately for himself, or for himself and his dependants or any of them.
There is more to the subparagraph, but that is the main part. The key concepts in

that definition are budgetary requirements, on the one hand, and resources available to the person on the other. The minister has made much of the fact that a difference between the needs test and the means test is that no monetary ceiling is established; we talk, rather, in terms of a person's budgetary requirements. If I may ask the minister to turn back to subclause (a) (i) he will see that there is another reference, which I think is relevant to my question. The reference is to "food, shelter, clothing, fuel, utilities, household supplies and personal requirements (hereinafter referred to as 'basic requirements')." On the side of what a person needs, as opposed to the side of what he has, there are two key phrases, "budgetary requirements" and "personal requirements". It must be obvious that the way in which one's budgetary requirements and personal requirements are defined will be crucial to the administration of this act. In subparagraph (g), which I read a moment ago, it would look as though this business of defining budgetary requirements has been tossed to the provinces, because the phrase used there is, "on the basis of a test established by the provincial authority that takes into account that person's budgetary requirements", and so on. The definition of these key phrases is to be left to the governor in council. I recognize that there is provision that if there is an order in council changing the definition of any matter that is important to the act, that change cannot be made until the province concerned consents to the making of such regulation that effects a change. But unless I misunderstand this language, it seems to me quite clear that in the first place the definition of the key
