speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext:
I should like to thank the committee very much for their kindness on this occasion.
Introducing the bill last year, the then minister of finance related it to the report of the Royal Commission on Banking and Finance and described the bill as a first step, but a substantial one, toward the general objectives proposed by the royal commission. The central theme of the report of the commission was that all our financial institutions, and particularly our banks, should have broader investing and borrowing powers than any of them had at the time the commission reported in order to achieve a more competitive and flexible financial system which will best serve the changing requirements of the Canadian economy.
The government decided that this central theme of the report should be taken as a long-term objective in the evolution of our financial system and noted that already progress had been made in that direction in our legislation relating to insurance, trust and loan companies. The view of the government remains that we must have a more competitive and flexible financial system which will best serve the changing requirements of the Canadian economy and the interests of all the people of Canada.
Bank Act
We are particularly concerned that the position of the smaller borrower be improved. This view is reflected in the substance of the bill that will be placed before you. Changing circumstances and further considerations have led the government to propose a number of changes in the bill that did not seem necessary or desirable a year ago. I shall mention in a moment the particular points of policy which we have changed, but first let me say something about the general background.
As part of the long-term policy to promote competition and flexibility in the financial system, it is desirable that progress be made in the legislation governing all financial institutions, both federal and provincial, and that the measures taken in regard to the various classes of institutions should be related to one another in such a way as to achieve this broad objective. Already we have done this in considerable measure in regard to our federal institutions, and I expect that we will be able to carry the process further, not only in our banking legislation and our legislation relating to trust and loan companies and insurance companies, but also in subsequent legislation regarding corporations and related matters, especially with regard to the disclosure of information.
Officials of the federal and provincial governments have recently met to discuss these and related matters. Out of this activity of both levels of government will come, I trust, a broadly integrated approach designed to improve our financial system as a whole so that it can better serve Canadian individuals and Canadian business.
I might also note that on May 27 I wrote to the provincial treasurers and ministers of finance of the provinces stating that I am prepared to convene a federal-provincial meeting on the subject of consumer credit and interest disclosure, which is so important to those Canadians who buy on the instalment plan or who borrow from finance companies. Although not all the provincial ministers have yet replied there is general support from those that have and I expect to be announcing a date for the conference some time in the near future.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
The constitutional situation relating to the jurisdiction of parliament over banking was reviewed by the minister last year in speaking on the resolution, and on second reading. I shall not endeavour to review it

July 5, 1S66
Bank Act
again this year. The bill we are now proposing relates only to the Bank Act without change in the jurisdictional scope of the existing legislation. It has, of course, been preceded by a bill to amend the Bank of Canada Act and will be followed by a revision of the Quebec Savings Banks Act. The then minister indicated that the government intended to give further consideration to possible changes in the clearing system, including suggestions made by the royal commission, and would bring forward legislation on this general subject, which seems clearly to come within parliament's jurisdiction over banking. We still have this in mind for a future year.
A system of insurance covering deposits in certain financial institutions would I think contribute substantially to our general objective of greater competition and flexibility in our financial system. It should be of help to new banks in getting started and growing, and it should be of help to trust companies and loan companies in developing their deposit business within the ambit of the legislation affecting them.
Events of last summer and the anxiety to which they gave rise concerning the position of a number of financial institutions have confirmed our belief that a system of deposit insurance would reassure the public as to the safety of deposits in insured financial institutions, and would provide in addition a residual source of liquidity for these institutions in circumstances where their liquidity might be in question. Such insurance would need to be accompanied by effective inspection and adequate regulation to safeguard the position of the insured institutions.
The government intends to introduce legislation during this session to establish a crown corporation in which the banks and other federally incorporated institutions would be required to have their deposits insured. Insurance premiums would have to be paid, although we believe these could be relatively low and would reflect the fact that the overall risk involved is likely to be small. The corporation would be authorized to insure the deposits of provincially incorporated institutions where this was desired by the institution and the provincial government concerned. The government will discuss this matter with the provincial authorities.
The bill introduced last year included a number of proposals intended to further the objective of greater flexibility in the working
[Mr. Sharp.I
of our financial institutions and greater competition between them. There were for example the proposals to enable banks to make conventional mortgage loans, to exempt mortgage loans from the maximum limit on interest rates, and to reduce the minimum cash ratio required against Canadian deposit liabilities. There were also provisions, to which I attach considerable importance, to prohibit agreements between the banks on interest rates both on deposits and on loans, and to prohibit bank mergers unless approval by the government has been obtained. Similar measures are included in the bill which it is our intention to introduce at the time of the approval of this resolution. In some cases there have been changes of detail. In addition, however, the present bill contains several further changes which will enable the banks to give better service to the public in circumstances which should increase competition among banks and between banks and other financial institutions.
The first of these changes is one to which I have referred in introducing the Bank of Canada Act. It is to accept in principle the recommendation of the royal commission that the cash reserves required on notice or term deposits should be lower than that on demand deposits. This will enable the banks to compete more actively with other institutions for term deposits. The weighted average cash requirement, based on the present distribution of deposits, would be slightly less than the 7 per cent proposed as a uniform ratio in last year's bill. The bill will provide for a gradual transition to this lower cash reserve requirement.
It is also proposed to enable the banks to compete more actively with other institutions for longer term funds. Many of these other institutions borrow a substantial amount of their funds by issuing debentures, whereas banks have been restricted to accepting deposits. Many banks in the United States have been issuing debentures in recent years and there seems no reason why our banks should not be able to do so. It is proposed therefore to allow banks to issue debentures which in priority will be subordinated to deposit liabilities, limited in total amount in the case of each bank to one half of its paid up capital and rest fund. This further source of funds should benefit bank borrowers generally.
The other major change which has been made in the bill is in respect of the ceiling on interest rates. The bill introduced last year
July 5, 1966

would have continued the existing 6 per cent limit. The minister stated, and I am quoting from his speech on second reading:
If at some future time there should be a general rise in world interest rates which would make these proposals unworkable, the government would reconsider the 6 per cent limit.
In fact there has been a general and substantial rise in interest rates in the western world. In the past year the rate of discount in our treasury bills has increased by about one and one quarter per cent, the rate of interest on long term corporate bonds has increased about three quarters of one per cent, and the rate of interest on conventional mortgages has increased by the same amount or somewhat more. As hon. members of the house know, interest rates in the United States and in Europe have increased substantially.
When the bill was introduced last year, the prime rate of interest on loans made by the banks was 5J per cent. The ceiling of 6 per cent, therefore, did not directly affect the prime rate. Its main effect was to limit the ability of Canadians to obtain the more risky or more expensive kinds of loans from the banks.
Now the general increase in interest rates has brought the prime rate of interest on loans made by banks up to the maximum rate permitted by law. All flexibility is gone. No variation in interest rate is possible to take into account the credit standing of the various borrowers, or other circumstances which would normally have a bearing on the interest rate. For all borrowers in the country, other than the Government of Canada, with perhaps minor exceptions, bank credit is now the cheapest source of credit available. Bank loans are in fact being rationed. In practice, this means that larger borrowers who could and should be seeking funds in the market are obtaining funds from the banks which would otherwise be available to the small borrower.
The royal commission had some pertinent observations to make on this kind of situation. I quote a few sentences from the report:
The distorting effects of the 6 per cent ceiling have been most acute in periods of credit restraint when the banks have been prevented from raising their rates on loans and deposits in line with market forces. At such times they cannot compete equally for funds and thus have no choice but to resort to arbitrary rationing procedures in their lending. The problem is further complicated by the fact that borrowers tend to press in on the banks because their lending rates remain artificially attractive while others rise.
Bank Act
There is no doubt at all what our long-term policy should be. The government accepts the view of the royal commission-and I quote again-that-
-the ceiling stands in the way of flexible lending by the banks in that it frequently prevents them from making loans on which higher rates must be charged to cover administrative costs and risks. Obviously, this is to the banks' disadvantage; more importantly, however, it discriminates against borrowers such as small businesses which, if they are to obtain funds at all, must turn to other lenders which charge rates well above those the banks would ask if free to do so. The banks have only been able to compete in the personal instalment loan market-in which they have substantially improved the facilities and lowered the average cost of funds-because the authorities have accepted what some might argue is a breach of the spirit of the 6 per cent law. This, however, is not an argument for forcing the banks out of this business, but is instead one for amending an outdated law.
That is the end of the quotation from the royal commission.
I also draw the attention of the house to the Second Annual Review of the Economic Council of Canada, published in December, 1965. In their conclusions and recommendations relating to monetary policy, the council said:
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
At the same time, the instabilities which have arisen in Canada's financial markets during the past year urge a careful reconsideration of both the needs and possible methods for improving and strengthening Canada's existing framework of financial institutions. More generally, to minimize distortions and instabilities in credit and financial markets and to ensure easier access by homebuilders, consumers and small business to credit, various recommendations of the Royal Commission on Banking and Finance deserve careful attention -including measures to promote more competitive credit conditions and removal of the arbitrary 6 per cent interest rate ceiling which currently forces many small borrowers into loans at much higher rates.
That is a quotation from the second and most recent report of the Economic Council. The clear message of both the Royal Commission and the Economic Council is that Canadians should not confuse the shadow with the substance. The present bank interest ceiling which appears to some to protect the smaller borrower in fact only protects those who are fortunate enough to be able to obtain bank credit, and forces the others to seek funds from other sources at higher cost.
The house will be aware, however, that the Porter commission made its report in 1964 at a time of comparative ease in credit conditions and that even in the months since the

July 5, 1966
Bank Act
Economic Council prepared its Second Annual Review there has been a strong surge of inflationary forces which has made it necessary to permit rising demands for credit to have an impact on credit conditions.
The puzzling problem is to decide what should be done in the changed and abnormal circumstances which now prevail when general economic conditions require that the expansion of credit be restrained. Although there is an economic case for removing the ceiling, even now we think this would be unwise, if only because the transition to unrestricted competition under present abnormal conditions could be abrupt and substantial and might well cause serious apprehension.
After considerable discussion-

speechtext:
-after very considerable discussion, the government has reached the conclusion that the law should provide for an objective test, in accordance with which the ceiling on interest rates will be removed when credit conditions have become substantially easier and when the present abnormal conditions that involve widespread rationing do not prevail. In the meantime, however, we feel the maximum rate should be adjustable to reflect changes in the general level of interest rates, which will help to reduce some of the distortions and injustices produced by the present rigid ceiling.
The interim arrangement in the bill making the ceiling adjustable should alleviate some of the consequences of the present situation in which the banks are the cheapest source of credit for larger borrowers. Some of these larger borrowers should be induced by this change to borrow in the securities market where rates are now moderately above the present ceiling rate on bank loans and this should enable the banks to lend more to other customers. Smaller borrowers who do not have the credit standing to borrow from the banks at a 6 per cent rate should have a better opportunity to get loans from the banks, instead of having to resort to other more expensive sources of credit.
Those who put their savings into bank deposits rather than other forms should be able to get a better return-particularly on the smaller deposits which have not benefited so far from the competition which has led to

higher rates on large corporate deposits which can be handled at less cost. In general, we shall be making a start toward the more competitive system which can be brought into effect when the current abnormal credit situation relaxes.
At an earlier stage of consideration of this question, an arrangement had been suggested to me by which the ceiling on rates would be removed on larger loans but retained temporarily on smaller ones. I came to the conclusion some weeks ago, that we should offer no inducement or even excuse for banks to favour larger borrowers in the allocation of credit at this time when the total amount must be under restraint. Consequently the formula proposed in the bill treats large and small borrowers alike.

subtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext:
In our opinion the best available basis from which to fix the maximum rate and eventually to measure the credit conditions under which the ceiling should be removed is the average market yield on short term government bonds. While several alternatives have been considered, the formula that is being submitted is reasonably simple and responsive to underlying credit conditions. I hope that when the bill is before the standing committee on finance, trade and economic affairs, to which I intend to ask that it be referred, the formula which is proposed will be examined with care to ensure that it is the best alternative to achieve our objectives.
Naturally, no one can say just when general interest rates will decline to the point that will release the ceiling on bank interest rates. I would hope it would come sooner rather than later, so that the proper development and evolution of our financial system as a whole can proceed on the basis of effective competition. Meanwhile, the provisions relating to mortgage lending, which have been somewhat modified from those in the bill of last year, will permit a greater measure of competition forthwith in this field, and this, I am sure, will be welcomed by the public. The bill will also permit continuing competition in the field of unsecured personal loans where the competition of the banks has resulted in a reduction of the rates paid for consumer credit. The experience with these consumer loans is, I think, an indication of the beneficial influence we can expect over the longer term by competition between the banks and other institutions.
July 5, 1966

Turning now to other matters being dealt with in the present bill, I would note that the government has decided to leave unchanged the provision in the present Bank Act that new banks shall be established only by special act of parliament. In last years' bill it had been proposed that new banks be incorporated by letters patent with the House of Commons having the right to nullify such letters patent within a stated period of time. After considering all the circumstances that could be involved, it has appeared to us that this long standing authority should remain with parliament. However, if further discussion on this point should indicate a general feeling that incorporation by letters patent is preferable, the government would be prepared to consider an amendment along these lines. Under either provision we would favour the establishment of more banks as a means of increasing competition.
The clause in last year's bill which would limit the over-all size of a bank in which one shareholder has a substantial interest-that is, a minimum of a 25 per cent interest-by reference to the amount of its authorized capital, has been continued in this bill. A bank which is dominated by one large shareholder, particularly if that one is an able and aggressive foreign bank, is not in the same position as other banks whose shares are held by many investors and which naturally have to increase their capital and issue additional shares from time to time as their business expands. The government does not believe that any bank should be an exception to the general situation in this respect. This measure of control need not involve any inequity.
One other change should probably be mentioned at this time. On second reading of last year's bill, the minister indicated government willingness to consider an amendment which would permit certain agencies of provincial governments, such as pension funds, to acquire modest amounts of bank shares perhaps on a non-voting basis. It has been decided to include this change in the present bill so that certain types of government funds will be able to acquire bank shares on a non-voting basis subject to the same over-all 10 per cent limit for the funds of any one government as applies in the case of other shareholders.
Provisions in the bill of last year limited to 10 per cent the number of voting shares that a bank would be permitted to own in any other corporation and limited to one-fifth the proportion of directors of a corporation who could be directors of any one bank. These 23033-4581
Bank Act
provisions we propose to continue and in addition, after the ceiling on the loans interest rate is removed and the banks have come into more direct competition with other deposit-taking institutions, this bill would provide that a director of any such institution, sometimes referred to as a near-bank, will not be permitted to become a director of a bank.
Finally I come to a point that has been the subject of much controversy at the time of previous revisions of the Bank Act. I have reached the conclusion that the shareholders of a bank and the public are entitled to have more complete information with regard to the financial operations of our banks and, for this purpose, this bill contains provisions which will require each bank for the first time to disclose in its annual financial statements the amount of its so-called inner reserves that have been created out of taxable income and the amount of its realized profits and losses during the year on investments and loans. The question of the extent to which the banks may create reserves free of taxation I am leaving until we have had an opportunity to receive and study the report of the Carter commission.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
In addition to the more important matters which have been mentioned, there will be a number of minor changes as compared with the bill which was introduced last year. The time available for discussion and comment has enabled us to propose detailed improvements of a technical nature.
I should like to re-emphasize the determination of the government that the fresh winds of competition shall permeate our system of banking and finance. We are determined that the system shall operate in the interests of the greatest number of Canadian consumers and businessmen. We are determined, in particular, that the interests of the small borrower and the small businessman shall be protected and furthered. We believe that the most effective way to achieve these ends is to encourage and to enforce competition. In this view, the government is supported by the Royal Commission on Banking and Finance and by the Economic Council of Canada. If there are many competing sources of loan funds and many institutions freely competing for the custom of the consumer, we are convinced that he cannot help but benefit.

July 5, 1966
Bank Act
May I, in conclusion, review some of the measures that we are proposing today to bring about the competitive conditions in our financial system that I have been describing.
1.	We propose that banks should not, after July 1971, be able to hold more than 10 per cent of the voting stock of any Canadian corporation, including what are popularly known as near-banks with which the chartered banks will be competing for deposits and loans.
2.	We propose a number of measures which will cut through the system of interlocking directorates. For example-
(a)	a director of one bank may not be a director of another bank
(b)	not more than one-fifth of the directors of the board of any single Canadian corporation may sit as directors of any one bank. This will produce a considerable revolution.
(c)	after the interest ceiling has been lifted, no director of any near-bank such as trust and loan companies that accept deposits from the public may become a director of a bank.
3.	Agreements among banks on interest rates on both loans and deposits will be prohibited. Mergers of banks will continue to require the approval of the government. In other words, the main underlying principles of the Combines Investigation Act will apply to banks.
4.	In order to provide maximum flexibility and to ensure that the banks can serve the smaller and riskier borrower as well as the larger and stronger, we intend that the present interest rate ceiling be eventually removed. This will occur when credit conditions have eased sufficiently to ensure that borrowers will benefit from competition. In the meantime, a ceiling realistically related to general interest rates will be maintained.
5.	We propose to require the banks to reveal to the public for the first time their inner reserves created out of taxable income.
6.	In order that the important questions affecting consumer credit may be examined in relation to all credit-granting institutions, I intend to call a federal-provincial conference in the near future to deal with this matter.
7.	We propose to strengthen substantially the competitive position of the so-called near-banks through a system of deposit insurance. This will increase their ability to attract deposits and strengthen public confidence in them.
8.	The proposed system of deposit insurance will help promote the creation of new

banks by strengthening them in the early stages of their development.
9.	We propose to allow banks to make mortgage loans. When the banks entered the personal loan field a few years ago, the interest rates paid by small borrowers were reduced. We expect the same beneficial effect from more competition in the mortgage field.
10.	We propose to establish new flexible and reduced cash reserve requirements to enable banks to compete more actively with other institutions for loans and deposits.
These changes now being proposed in the act, as well as others to which I have referred, will permit, encourage and indeed require competition. The Canadian banking system is world renowned for its financial integrity and stability. Our banks now must become more flexible in their ways of doing business and learn to compete more effectively among themselves and with other institutions. It is my intention that the prohibition of agreements on interest rates shall be enforced. I would hope and expect that there will be competition in the rates charged on loans and in the interest rates and other terms offered on deposits. I would hope that we will see more frequent changes in the rates of interest that they charge, and that they offer, in response to market changes. I do not believe that competition should merely extend to the quality of service. There seems to be more room for individual banks to differ in the nature of the services they render. For example, it is surprising that banks have experimented so little with variations of office hours.
The bill will provide a blueprint for competition. I trust that in the next decade we will witness a significant modernization of our banking system.
When the bill has received second reading, I propose that it should be referred to the standing committee on finance, trade and economic affairs for detailed study.

Mr. Chairman, the committee has listened to a recital by the minister of a variety of generalities. He has refused to give particulars. He asks the house to accept his general view as expressed in the resolution. By his attitude he has indicated that we are supposed to accept a resolution unexplained and apparently unexplainable, a proceeding as unusual as it is unjustified.
>
(8:40 p.m.)
I say at once to the minister that he has simply placed before the house a hodgepodge of uncertain plans with a few definite conclusions, unchanged from last year, and he has asked the house in faith to accept from him the assurance that if the resolution is passed there will be revealed to the house various matters which up to the present time have not been elucidated or explained in any way.
I am going to speak for a moment on the general purposes of Bank Act revisions and then deal with several of the matters to which the minister alluded. All of us are agreed that we must share in this nation in the maintenance of confidence in our financial system. A royal commission was set up by the government, of which I had the
Bank Act
honour to be the head, under Chief Justice Dana Porter. It studied the banking situation for 30 months. In May of 1965 this government, after 11 months of study, brought proposals before the house and the country with the objective of a more open and competitive banking system and another objective, to remove the restrictions which impede response to new situations and to explain the need for revision long overdue.
A commission is set up and it makes recommendations, and I am going to refer to that in general in a moment. The government found itself in a dispute between the forces of the hon. member for Davenport and the present minister. According to the press, tremendous controversies have sprung up. Unity at any price is apparently the objective. What amendments have finally been determined? Out of chaos and uncertainty the government produces formulae of compromise. I do not have to go beyond this evening's issue of the Toronto Star, which is accepted in Liberal circles as the essence of all that is good, proper and appropriate.
The heading in that newspaper tonight is "When Marchand and Sharp Both Threatened to Quit". In the last few weeks there has apparently been a tremendous division. The article written by Martin Goodman states:
The threatened resignation from the federal cabinet of immigration minister Jean Marchand was the hidden factor that caused Prime Minister Lester Pearson to order a delay in bringing forward the revised Bank Act two weeks ago . . .
And, after finance minister Mitchell Sharp forced Pearson to reverse that decision by threatening to resign himself, one of the things that soothed Marchand and kept him in the cabinet was Sharp's agreement to okay increased aid to the aged-but only in the fall.
I emphasize the word "soothed", because when one sees some of the recommendations that were made by the minister this evening it becomes obvious that there was a great deal of soothing syrup used by the minister to bring about a feeling of equanimity. The article states:
One of the things that soothed Marchand and kept him in the cabinet was Sharp's agreement to okay increased aid to the aged-but only in the fall.
What a government this is. We hoped this afternoon to hear an explanation by the Minister of National Health and Welfare as to what the plans are to end poverty. This article in the Toronto Star states:
This hidden relationship between two of the government's major decisions-the removal of the 6

July 5, 1966
Bank Act
per cent interest ceiling in the Bank Act and $30 aid to needy pensioners-has been pieced together over the last week . . .
It is a tale of two threatened resignations, of a holiday weekend spent in feverish negotiations and, at the end, of a political saw-off that saw both Sharp and health minister Allan MacEachen emerge with important cabinet victories.
What a revelation as to the way in which these people in office produce policies for Canada. The article then states:
The Bank Act legislation is ready to be presented to the Commons and, at an opportune time, MacEachen is to announce the government's intention to give more aid to the aged.
The announcements will culminate six months of political manoeuvring by Sharp and MacEachen to win cabinet approval of their goals.
That is a magnificent story and it shows how utterly hypocritical is the attitude taken by the government in connection with this matter. The article then states:
At one point, MacEachen led 26 unhappy MPs into Pearson's office to plead for more assistance.
What a government. It goes on to state:
Early in June, Sharp finally got his way with the Bank Act.
Although the majority of the cabinet had political qualms, Pearson gave his approval . . .
Overworked and under pressure, disillusioned with some of the direction the so-called reformed party was taking, Marchand regarded removal of the interest ceiling as the last straw.
We know now that the ceiling is not being removed, so apparently all of those discordant elements almost threw them, you might say, into the cave of Adullam. The Old Testament speaks of the gathering together of the afflicted, the uncertain and the fearful. These people met together in a cave of Adullam.
The article then states:
At any rate, Sharp, conscious of the need to soothe ruffled feelings within the party over the Bank Act, finally agreed to an increase.
That is a reference to the increase to pensioners of $30 a month. Mr. Goodman then writes:
Meantime Sharp, too, was caught up in the effort to persuade Marchand to stay in the cabinet.

They met together-the most frightful commentary on a hapless government that has ever been given to the people of any country on a matter as serious as amending the Bank Act. They waited. They thought. They compromised. They brought together those on the left and those on the right. Within the cabinet there was disagreement. Outside the cabinet-and it is the only time in Canadian history that there has been a cabinet and a shadow cabinet in the same government-the shadow cabinet under the member for Davenport, with the assistance of the member for Outremont-Saint-Jean, pulled one way. Neither of these former ministers is in the chamber tonight.
Is that a way to bring about amendments to the Bank Act, for a government to play around with this problem for 11 months? They postponed the matter and this evening instead of formidable and important changes to meet the challenges of the changing economy we have a series of uncertain, unstable compromises designed to hold unity in the government among those who support it, regardless of consequences to the country.
Let us examine what the commission recommended. It recommended the abolition of the statutory 6 per cent interest ceiling on bank loans. It recommended allowing mortgage lending by banks. It recommends that all institutions doing banking business be brought under the federal Bank Act. There was no suggestion of that whatsoever in what the minister said this evening. There was a suggestion that if companies incorporated under provincial legislation, and the province which they are incorporated, decide to accept deposit insurance, it will be brought into effect.
The royal commission recommended full disclosure of interest rates on all credit. There is nothing in what the minister said to give effect to that recommendation. The Porter commission went on to say that nearbanks should be brought under the Bank Act. This could be brought about by agreement with the provinces. It recommended that there be action taken to stop concentration in the financial community. There is no awareness of the other matters that were recommended, excepting fuller financial disclosure by corporations. The commission might just as well never have sat. What has been produced is simply an arrangement whereby the highest common factor relating to changes and amendments is to be recognized. The
July 5, 1966

caucus, according to the press references, would not stand for removal of the interest ceiling. And what do we get? We get the production of a plan as outlined by the minister, and he will not even give us the full detail.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is well to keep silent rather than make interruptions in a voice and manner that cannot be heard. The caucus convened. In February he sent his parliamentary secretary to placate the members of caucus, according to the press. On February 1 it was reported that in the first week of January the hon. member for Davenport sent a letter to the finance minister setting
Bank Act
out his views and warning the finance minister that he might have to state them publicly. He suggested in the letter, as reported in the press, that the Minister of Finance should consult him before acting; but the minister did not do so.
It is a strange situation. Where tonight is the member for Davenport? Have the ideas he uttered a year ago, accepted by the Prime Minister and the government as orthodox finance, become unorthodox in the last year? What has brought about the change? What has happened? As one press man with the Toronto Globe and Mail who seems always to know what is going on in Liberal circles said on February 15, there really was not a revolt among the members of the Liberal party. He said there was no revolt. They could not revolt because-and the second "because" was this-the minister had not yet declared his position on the interest ceiling. He went on to express the assured hope, in consequence of discussions with an individual usually most reliable, that the minister was going to insist on the removal of the 6 per cent ceiling. He did say as did the minister this evening, that the former minister of finance, the hon. member for Davenport, had stated that if at some future time there should be a general rise in world interest rates which would make these proposals unworkable, the government would consider the 6 per cent limit. What have they done? Are they going to bring about competition, to which the minister paid lip service? Will they ensure that the near-banks and trust companies are brought under federal supervision which could be achieved by arrangement with the provinces? What has been the actual reason for the concessions and changes that have been made? There were two essential issues: first, the ceiling- now forgotten.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
All through the last few months we have been following the situation. We read in the Toronto Globe and Mail of February 15 "Interest ceiling bedevils Liberals". Then, on April 15, it said: "Sharp likely to remove 6 per cent bank interest". On May 26 it said: "Liberals split over banking act changes". On May 21 Victor Mackie of the Winnipeg Free Press wrote "Bank rate to be raised". On May 27 the Toronto Star wrote "P.M. follows 'Walter Sharp' line". On June 31 it wrote "Bank act is coming and the 6 per cent ceiling on bank loans will be lifted".

July 5, 1966
Bank Act
The minister produced this unsatisfactory compromise which bears no regard whatsoever to the recommendations of the Porter commission. Where is the courage about which the Prime Minister spoke on April 23, 1963? Where has it gone? It has certainly not come to rest in the soul and heart of the Minister of Finance.
Arguments have been advanced on all sides in support of the freeing of the bank rate. The public argument is that it would permit the banks to enhance their profit position; that it would compel a shift to higher rates; that it would increase the cost of doing business. On the other hand the counter-argument is advanced that if the ceiling were removed, it would actually bring about expansion and development, would be beneficial to the small borrower and would assure depositors of higher rates.
What has the government done after all these months and months of gestation? It produced after much postponement a monstrosity on the subject of interest rates. It would have taken courage to have followed the recommendations of the Porter commission, but the minister's stand in the election campaign was the 6 per cent interest rate ceiling should be removed. He told us he did not hold that view, but all I can say to him is that in the city of Toronto there are many of those in high finance who must have misunderstood what the minister had said.

They say: "If we don't do something we will be in trouble. Isn't there some formula that we can produce that will fool everybody?" That is what they have done.
Talk about a bigamous government-a government committing political bigamy. It is married to those who want an increase in interest rates and it is betrothed to those who oppose it. It is an amazing performance, and we are asked to take seriously the recommendations of the minister in this connection.
The delay in bringing in these amendments has been harmful to Canada. It has been

Mr. Chairman, to begin with I think I should say that I am not particularly interested in the details of the real or imagined or reported split and division within the government and the Liberal party. I have never been interested in the squalid details of domestic quarrels. I am concerned with what the minister told us and even more concerned with what he has not told us tonight.
In fact, Mr. Chairman, we have had a remarkable exhibition today of two cabinet ministers both performing a sort of dance of the seven veils, and refusing to take the last veil off, out of modesty one presumes. Perhaps they realize that they were intellectually related under the seventh veil. At any rate, we are not told. One can be more kind and suggest that what we have seen has been a very skilful operation of the old pea and shell game. We are asked to guess what is under the shell, which pea is under it and which shell it is under. We cannot say, of course, because we are kept in the dark.
Frankly, Mr. Chairman, I have been very disappointed in the minister's presentation. I did not expect that I would altogether agree with him but I did hope that I was going to hear a reasoned case for the adoption of a certain policy, about which I might well have had some reservation. But we did not get that tonight. We had a number of rather discursive remarks suggesting certain things might be done, but nothing definitive and positive was told us.
The question of the 6 per cent interest rate is, of course, one which has engaged the public attention, and I am surprised that the Minister of Finance was not able to marshal respectable intellectual arguments in support of the rmoval of the 6 per cent limit and to present to this house a policy of substituting some other method of control of the banking system.
Instead of that he took refuge in extraordinarily vague statements. We were told that a ceiling will be retained-a ceiling. We are not told where it is, how high up it is, or what the ceiling is. There was mention of some approximation between the permitted interest rate and the average short-term yield on government bonds. But again, no definition

and no suggestion as to who was going to impose the regulatory functions upon this particular issue.
While I have not been entirely persuaded that it is essential at this particular time to remove the 6 per cent ceiling on bank interest rates, I am quite aware, of course, of the arguments in favour of a greater degree of flexibility in interest rates by the chartered banks. But having said that, sir, I think we then have to face something else that the minister refuses to face.
In fact, his speech tonight was in main a complete denial of something that I thought he would have recognized, something which I am sure most people in Canada, and I would suggest almost the entire business community in Canada, are all too well aware of, namely that the banking system of Canada is a monopoly. It is sheer nonsense and poppycock to talk of competition in our banking system. It is a monopoly, and I am not at all sure that it is not a good thing that it is a monopoly. It is a monopoly that has been given a privileged position in our society and our economy, to the degree that no bank in Canada can possibly fail, because no government can allow any bank to fail.
Twelve years ago, at the last revision of the Bank Act, I asked the then Governor of the Bank of Canada whether, in his opinion, it was possible at that time for a bank in Canada to fail. Mr. Towers, who was the Governor at the time, with commendable banker's caution, said well, he did not want to give a categorical statement that it was impossible for a bank to fail in Canada, but he would say that it was extremely unlikely and could only take place in conditions of virtual economic collapse.
So I think we have to face this fact: We have a monopoly with ironclad guarantees of survival and protection from any disaster. Because this is the case, we then must have some method of controlling it. If the minister is not prepared to devise a more sophisticated method of controlling it than he has suggested tonight, then I would submit to you, sir, that the safety of the Canadian people impels us to insist on the maintenance of the present 6 per cent limit, clumsy, unselective and inadequate as it may be, as a means of controlling this monopoly which has a privileged position and which, in the final analysis, is and must be supported by the Canadian government and the Canadian taxpayer. As I say, I was surprised that the minister appeared to be unable to bring
July 5, 1966

forward a more sophisticated approach to this problem.
It would appear to me that having granted, as those who have studied the matter must grant, that there must be some greater flexibility in our banking system, we must then turn our attention to this problem of just how to exercise the controls that we must exercise on this monopoly. I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that the answer will have to be the institution of a regulatory body before which the banks will have to present a case for an increase in interest rates; that this regulatory body will have to have the power to control the whole range of interest rates to prevent the banking monopoly from demonstrating its monopolistic character in the most disastrous way by discriminating between various classifications of borrowers.
I cannot understand why the minister continues to talk nonsense, using such lovely phrases as "the fresh winds of competition blowing through our banking system". Is the minister going to blow those fresh winds himself? Is this the case of the wolf in the child's tale-that "he huffed and he puffed till he blew the house down"? I am afraid that the minister will huff and puff but will never succeed in blowing any fresh winds of competition into an industry which, by its very nature, is a monopoly.
The minister talks nonsense about how he will have the banks brought up for examination under the Combines Investigation Act. If the minister does not know that that is nonsense, then he has no business to be Minister of Finance. If he does know, then he has no business to have made this ridiculous suggestion to us.
What is he going to do in this regard? Is he boing to call the president of the Royal Bank of Canada and the president of the Bank of Nova Scotia into his office and say: "Look, boys, I have discovered that each of you has made loans at 6J per cent. Obviously this is a combine. You must have different interest rates, otherwise I will charge you under the Combines Investigation Act"? What utter nonsense. Why produce these ridiculous straw men, suggesting that you can do something with a monolithic-and it is-and monopolistic institution?
I am not holding back against the idea of the banking system in Canada being an integrated system, virtually a monopoly in the performance of its functions, because it must be stable. There must be some uniformity. To suggest that we are going to gain anything by 23033-4591
Bank Act
pretending that we can bring the banks under the Combines Investigation Act is not worthy of the Minister of Finance of this country; it is sheer nonsense and an insult to our intelligence.
I would very much urge on the Minister of Finance, Mr. Chairman, that before he brings this bill before the house, or, having brought it before the house, before he appears before the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs in support of it, he seriously consider devising a much more sophisticated manner of ensuring flexibility in our major lending institutions and protection for the borrowers of money under the Canadian banking system. That this could be done I have not the slightest doubt. A regulatory body that could perform these functions could be easily devised, and it would not be without precedent in our history.
We have been faced with this sort of thing before, and on every occasion when we were faced with an industry that was in a monopolistic or semi-monopolistic situation, the operations of which were of great concern to the whole economy, we have established regulatory bodies. We have established such things as the Board of Transport Commissioners and the National Energy Board. These bodies were meant to deal with exactly the same powers and privileges that are enjoyed by the banking system, though not quite so wide; therefore there is even more necessity for such a provision under the Bank Act.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
The minister also tells us that he is going to protect us from the evils of competition by making it illegal for the director of one bank to be the director of another bank, or to be the director of a near-bank. In July of 1971-and I do not know why July, 1971 should be the date chosen-banks can hold only 10 per cent of any other corporation's stock.
I wonder whether the Minister of Finance is so naive as never to have heard of a breed of animals that used to be known in Great Britain as guinea pigs? They sit on the boards of directors of large corporations, not knowing anything about them. Very often they are impoverished nobility in need of extra income. They sit on boards representing certain interests in the operation of that corporation, and they of course give the whole thing an air of respectability. Their chief function is to sit there on behalf of interests that do not want to come into the open. Can you imagine for a moment that

you are going to be able to root out every guinea pig that takes a position on a board of directors in defiance of this ruling by the Minister of Finance? If certain interests want those guinea pigs on boards, they will have them.
The minister tells us that he thinks more banks will permit more competition. I suppose "permit" is the right word. He did not tell us why he thought that more banks would ensure more competition, because I suppose he felt that was too much even for the House of Commons to swallow. We are all aware of what has happened to the banking system in Canada, and it is very difficult to persuade us that by establishing a number of banks you thereby establish competition. You may be able to develop a more effective system, providing a wider range of services, but as to competition, no; there can be and will be no competition. When the minister continually insists that it is going to be possible to permit competition, I think he is insulting our intelligence. Instead of doing that, instead of wasting his time, he should have been devoting his intellect to really dealing with the problems of banks in the modern world. If he is not prepared to do that, I want to say this, that we must retain the 6 per cent clumsy club of control that we now have over the banks.
If he does not provide a workable, sophisticated method of control, and one that does not give relief to the banks in order that they make more money, it will not be only the opposition in this chamber that he will have at his throat, it will be the people who write letters to me and, I imagine, to all members of this house on this question of the removal of the 6 per cent. The people writing will be business people and individuals viewing with great alarm and despair the thought that the banks are going to be set free to take an even greater tribute from our economy than they are taking at the present time.
Indeed, there was one phrase the minister used that rather disturbed me. I shall have to see Hansard tomorrow to find out exactly the text, but the minister spoke about carrying out his plans without changing the scope of the Bank Act.
The Porter Commission-and I have been waiting for an opportunity to say this for some time-made a very unsatisfactory report. It was one of the most poorly compiled technical reports I have ever seen. It was a mess. It left a great many loose threads dangling in the air. But it said that the

near-banks should be brought under the Bank Act. It did not say how that was to be done. It made one suggestion: that there should be a definition of banking that would bring the near-banks under the Bank Act. I think that might be possible. However, I should first want to refer to a constitutional lawyer to find out whether we can remove from provincial control an operation that is licensed by the provincial government, merely by defining that operation in this parliament. I do not know whether it is possible. Certainly, you will not be able to bring these concerns under banking legislation, in order to control them, until something like that is done.
I think we must be careful not to take any action that will encourage the growth of these so-called near-banks in our banking functions. Despite all the faults of our banks, despite their greed, if you like, and their ruthlessness, the minister is quite right; the banks and banking system of Canada are extremely efficient, and we should not encourage less efficient institutions to carry on functions that should be carried on by the chartered banks of Canada. Unless we are prepared to bring the near-banks under control, I do not know how we shall prevent their unrestricted operation. Apparently they will be enticed to come under federal control to some extent by the offer of taking part in the insured deposit system, which is to be carried out by a crown corporation, about which we heard very little.
I feel, Mr. Chairman, that as the minister has seen fit to withhold his confidence from us, not telling us anything about what this legislation is going to be, but merely offering disturbing hints in much the same way as the Minister of National Health and Welfare did this afternoon, and because it is extremely important for members of this house to discuss the possible consequences of the legislation that is still locked in the minister's mind that we have been abused. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I am nearly through. I also noticed that in his statement the minister warned us that in the future, in the studies made concerning banking reforms, provincial governments and companies will be able to acquire bank shares subject to a 10 per cent limit, but unfortunately, he added: not voting shares.
Mr. Chairman, I think this will be a matter of discussion during consideration of this bill and we intend to put our opinions forward in that connection. As we will base ourselves on the Royal Commission on Banking during these discussions on banking reform, I hope the minister will allow for once the Bank of Canada to take its true place in our financing system.
The analysis of our financial system has shown that the Bank of Canada plays second fiddle; I therefore submit that, during the future studies, the Bank of Canada recapture its natural part, the leading outstanding part it should play in our financial system, in short that it be called upon to finance all public sectors, in order to leave to chartered banks the financing of private sectors.
Thus we will no longer see chartered banks lack credit every season. When everyone is in his place and does his part, we will say that the Bank of Canada is the national bank; it must finance national affairs, national departments and not look after private affairs. I believe, Mr. Chairman, that as soon as we begin to study this bill, we will be able to shed some more light on the banking system, so as to inform everyone.

Mr. Chairman, first of all I should like to thank the members of the committee for their indulgence in sitting past our regular adjournment hour so that I could make a few comments respecting the statement made by the Minister of Finance when he introduced this resolution. I would say at the outset that while we can agree with many of the objectives stated by the Minister of

Finance when he introduced the resolution, it seems to me that there is not very much in the remarks he made that would appear to give effect to those objectives.
For example, the minister talks about this new Bank Act being a blueprint for competition. From the information that we have thus far respecting the amendments which will be in the new Bank Act when we receive it after first reading, there does not appear to me to be very much that will assure any greater competition in the field of banking, particularly in so far as the chartered banks of Canada are concerned.
I want to state very briefly that we certainly hope that the changes that will be in the bill when we see it are not changes or amendments or compromises, or whatever you wish to call them, that have come about because of divisions within the Liberal party. The amendments to the Bank Act are so important that this should not be a matter of compromise between any ministers of the crown in trying to bring in changes that are of benefit to Canada and Canadians generally.
I want also to say that I hope there is no substantive foundation to the press report that the right hon. Leader of the Opposition read from the Toronto Star, to the effect that these compromises came about as a result of sharp divisions of opinion between the Minister of Finance and the minister of manpower, because I believe that the old age pension, the Old Age Security Act and even the Canada Assistance Plan are far too important to have amendments based on some compromise that can be reached respecting the Bank Act.
We in this party agree that there ought to be more competition in the banking field. There is no question about that. But it seems to me we have not as yet heard from the Minister of Finance how he intends to achieve this end. Yet there has certainly been plenty of time because, for example, there were the 10 years that expired in 1964 when the Bank Act should have been revised. In addition to that, the Minister of Finance and his colleagues have had the benefit of not only the Royal Commission on Banking and Finance, that took some 30 months looking into this matter, but they also have the reports of two years from the Economic Council of Canada in which comments were made about banks and banking in this country. In addition, we are now two years overdue in coming to grips with the changes that

are needed in the Bank Act. Therefore I do not think the minister can plead that he has not had sufficient time to come forth with the kind of amendments that will make the banks and banking in Canada more effective and in keeping with modern requirements.
I was interested in the minister's comment that all financial institutions will be brought under the umbrella of the Bank Act and that to achieve this end he has issued an invitation to the provincial governments to come to a federal-provincial conference, in an attempt to work out some kind of agreement and arrangements as to how this will be done.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
I agree with the hon. member for Nanai-mo-Cowichan-The Islands when he suggested there might be some constitutional conflict in simply naming these other types of institutions that are close to banks, and thereby in fact requiring them to comply with the federal legislation. I am convinced that to bring a provincially organized institution within the terms of the federal act will be far more complex than that. However, Mr. Chairman, I suppose we will hear something more about this. I hope the Minister of Finance is prepared to tell this house what he intends to ask the provincial ministers of finance to do to bring these other institutions in line with a uniform banking policy.
The minister has also spoken about a crown corporation which would in fact provide insurance covering deposits, not only in banks but in some of these near banks. He suggested it would encourage people to place deposits in the banks. This may be true for some of the so-called near-banks, but all it will do with regard to chartered banks that are concerned will be to increase the cost of depositing.
I am therefore not impressed with the suggestion that the existing chartered banks in particular should require any kind of insurance for depositors. What is more, Mr. Chairman, I do not believe there is any satisfactory argument for insurance coverage jf deposits even in the new banks which may be formed in the immediate future because, as the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands suggested, when banks in this country receive a federal charter they are required to put forth such a substantial foundation that if they are to operate within the ambit of the existing Bank Act there is small likelihood of any insurance being required for those deposits. The only time it
Bank Act
would be necessary would be in case of a complete economic collapse of this country, and we certainly hope that this will never come to pass.
We also agree that chartered banks should be allowed a wider scope in the loans that they can make, such as mortgage loans and others. We were somewhat disappointed that the minister did not spell out some new conditions in this Bank Act which will legalize what we have considered to be a breach of the Bank Act in the statutory 6 per cent limit which has been set up to this time. I am speaking of small personal loans in particular. I am convinced it costs more to service this kind of loan and I am therefore prepared to consider, and perhaps to approve, some amendments to the Bank Act which would allow the banks to charge a slightly higher fee for such loans. I believe that some of those details should be spelled out in the act because at the present time the provisions of the act are being violated by the charging of a higher effective rate than that allowed by the statutory limit, and other ways, such as the date of discount and the date of repayment, and other similar practices. I do not believe that this is the proper way of increasing the limit even for those loans which in fact carry a higher service cost. I hope therefore that in the course of our debate on this bill we will evolve a provision spelling out these new conditions.
I agree, Mr. Chairman, that the banks should be allowed to raise funds in some way other than by deposits. As the minister suggested, they should be allowed to issue debentures. This is in keeping with the practices of some of the near-banks and I find it to be satisfactory. However, in so far as these small loans are concerned, I am not prepared to agree that the great growth of the nearbanks and other public financial institutions has been wholly due to the legislation, even as it is contained in the present Bank Act.
I believe that several years ago the chartered banks of this country failed to provide the kind of service that Canadians needed and wanted. Therefore, almost as a result of the default of the banks, these other types of institution have flourished in the personal loan field and small business loans. I think that perhaps in the last two or three years, or even a little longer than that, the banks finally woke up and realized there was a large, new market that they had missed which resulted in the growth of these other financial institutions. I believe we need to

recognize that the banks failed to provide the service that was desired.
The minister suggested that in so far as the statutory limit is concerned, it could not be changed suddenly. He did not say very much else about it except there would be some interim arrangement pending the complete release of the statutory limit. This interim arrangement will be tied to the effective rate on short term government bonds and will be set at some undisclosed percentage above that rate. I feel the minister should have and could have given this information to the house, because if you look over all the changes that have been suggested, this is the most important one with which he dealt. Surely the house ought to have heard what kind of formula is suggested, or at least what the percentage of spread was going to be over this so-called effective interest rate.
There are many other things that we want to discuss, such as this requirement concerning directorship and the percentage of stock that any individual may hold. However, there will be plenty of time to do that on second reading of the bill. I want to say again that while the minister calls this a blueprint for competition and he talks about the fresh winds of competition that will permeate the banking system, there is very little in what the minister said that will give effect to this statement. He did not say whether or not the prohibition against agreements so far as interest charges by the banks are concerned was going to be enforced by the Combines Investigation Act, or under some similar arrangement. If the minister means what he says, and he is going to give effect to it, then we will have to have some additional laws with some teeth in them. Otherwise, his suggestion that there will be competition between chartered banks is, in my opinion, simply so many words.
There has been no effective competition in the banking industry in the immediate past. There may have been a measure of competition between the managers of local branches, but so far as conditions generally are concerned, there has been no competition in the banking system. We do not see anything in the minister's statement that would indicate conditions are going to be any better. We would be interested in knowing, as quickly as possible, under what conditions the minister is going to release the statutory limit on interest altogether. He said this could not be done now because of current conditions in the financial market. We would like to know

when we can expect this information to be released. I hope the minister will come back to parliament for additional amendments before it is, in fact, released.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
I will not keep the committee longer because, as I said, I appreciate the indulgence shown me in permitting me to go beyond the regular adjournment hour. As I said when I began my remarks, we agree with many of the objectives of the minister, particularly the state objective that there needs to be more competition in the banking field. But up until now the explanation given by the Minister of Finance has failed to spell out how that competition is to be made effective.

NATURAL GAS-U.S. HEARING ON TRANSMISSION BETWEEN CANADIAN POINTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some ten years ago a proposal to build a natural gas pipe line from western to eastern Canada was the subject of considerable bitter debate in this house with far-reaching consequences. Nevertheless, the pipe line was approved and its subsequent operation has been a great success, so much so that just eight years later the capacity of the original line requires immediate expansion.
July 5. 1966

During the debate over this matter in 1956 Hansard indicates accord on one major related point, and that is the routing of the pipe line. Speaker after speaker from different parties stated his conviction that this should be all-Canadian. As a result, the line was built from Alberta through Saskatchewan, Manitoba, northern Ontario and thence to Toronto. It is claimed that the highest cost portion of that route was in northern Ontario, and this was known to be likely before construction began. But the decision of that day was to bear this additional capital cost, so as to keep this vital energy resource on Canadian soil and under Canadian control. And, Mr. Speaker, I say that this was a wise choice.
This year we face a similar decision. Trans-Canada Pipe Lines has applied for approval to build a second line, this time through the northern states. From the exit at Emerson, Manitoba, to the re-entrance at Sarnia, this facility would be on United States soil, subject forever to the control of the United States. Today it appears possible that all the sound arguments presented for an all-Canadian route may be in danger of being forgotten.
The public hearings before the National Energy Board of Trans-Canada's application were completed in March. We do not yet know what the decision might be, and quite properly the members of the National Energy Board will not indicate their reaction until their ruling is announced. I have confidence in the vast knowledge often displayed by the chairman and members of that board, but I rise tonight to bring this matter to the attention of the final Canadian authority, parliament itself, because I feel that it is a much too important decision to be made without discussion in this house. We are facing a major choice of principle in dealing with this application to place forever on foreign soil and under foreign control a major Canadian resource asset.
We are asked to accept this proposal, when there is an acceptable alternative course open to us which would retain this program as an all Canadian facility. Such an alternative does exist in looping and adapting the existing northern Ontario pipe line to provide the necessary increase in capacity. As a northwestern Ontario member I have a parochial viewpoint of course. We are conscious of the economic impact in our area of the capital expenditure of some $240 million to $260 million in northern Ontario if the existing line is looped.

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
Already our industries are using more than twice as much gas as was originally estimated. Several industries and communities in northwestern Ontario are not yet serviced by natural gas. A number are not assured of an adequate supply from the present line for immediate needs, let alone future expansions and new industrial growth.
So I will not deny a local bias. But I am also vitally concerned about the danger to the national interest, if the U.S. location is approved.
Beyond identifiable and concrete economic factors identified in light of present laws and attitudes of the United States, we feel concern about future change in those attitudes and regulations. Such changes might be difficult to foresee now, but in any number of ways, and at any time, they could present a threat to the transmission system and the Canadian public interest-if the line is built in the United States. The Canadian route would eliminate that worry and danger, which must be considered as an intangible but significant factor.
When I appeared before the National Energy Board in March I supported the intervention of the Fort William/Port Arthur and District Council to the Trans-Canada application. Among other comments, I specifically requested that, before a decision is rendered, there be made, published and publicly discussed, an independent cost analysis and comparison of the total economic effect of both routes. No reply or indication of reaction to my request has been given by the board. This, partly, gives rise to my concern and to my action in bringing this before parliament tonight.
We are told by Trans-Canada that the difference in capital cost between looping the existing northern Ontario system and building a new line through the United States could amount to over $30 million in favour of the United States route. Even if this were so, we say there is great wisdom in keeping th s all Canadian for the reasons I have already outlined.
In addition I should like to draw attention to these other disadvantages of the United States route: First, the amount of United States dollars that are going to have to be invested initially by Trans-Canada; second, the continuing drain of United States dollars required to be paid by Trans-Canada to Great Lakes Transmission, Trans-Canada's United States partner, which would own the United States pipe line in question. So, for

But, in final argument, I want to introduce an important new fact that to the best of my knowledge was not presented during the National Energy Board hearings. Throughout Trans-Canada has claimed that by taking the United States route as opposed to the looping of the northern system, natural gas would be delivered at a lower price to the consumer in eastern Canada.
Today, I am in possession of a brief that purports to refute that claim. This was prepared by the Panhandle Eastern Pipe Line Company of New York and the Trunkline Gas Company of Houston, Texas-both United States corporations. It was tabled with the Federal Power Commission, in opposition to Trans Canada's application to that United States regulatory body, and is a matter of record there.

The National Energy Board was set up in the late fifties to assess these projects in the Canadian interest and to take into account various technical aspects of the submissions made by the pipe line companies, by the producers and by the consuming utilities, most of them, in this case, being in eastern Canada. Normally, the governor in council will accept the recommendation of the National Energy Board. RESEARCH-SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON SPACE RESEARCH
speechtext:
I should like to direct the attention of the house to the substance of a question I raised on July 4 as will be found reported at page 7,128 of Hansard with reference to a policy on space research for this country and the present position of space research.
I suppose each generation has before it a special challenge which stands out from the others as being of special importance, possibly as expressing the spirit of the age itself. When we think of the 'sixties our attention will undoubtedly be turned to the whole question of space. Outer space is the frontier of this half of the twentieth century. Many of us have spent hours viewing with fascination some of the great adventures which have taken place in space brought to us by means of television. Unfortunately, even though Canada has in the past few years begun to work in the area of space research, public
July 5, 1966	COMMONS
opinion generally has been uninformed and it has certainly not been clear to myself, and, perhaps to other hon. members, that we have had a clearly defined policy in this regard.
Perhaps our policy can best be described as reflecting the attitude: Ignore it, and perhaps it will go away. Unfortunately, our space program, if it can be called that in terms of being in harmony with interests of the Canadian people, does not possess the spirit, the purpose, the direction or the policy we might like to see. Space research has been divided among many departments and organizations. The National Research Council and the Defence Research Board are two groups which have taken some part in it. There have been a number of university projects, the high altitude research project at McGill among them. We even And in a place like Churchill a space research project which is Canadian. At least, Canada pays the bill, though the people employed are for the most part Americans.
Frankly I am at a loss to know-after all we have not been in the space business very long-why we have not had more parliamentary interest and a definite outline of our policy with regard to space research. More recently we have instituted a Science Council; but space research is more than science. It involves communications, transportation, defence, and ramifications involving industry. It even has a cultural effect. This is such a large and important question not only to the world at large but even to this country that we must not wait too long before we institute a parliamentary committee to examine this in detail. We are losing many well-trained people. I am told that only one person in ten who applies to work in space research in this country finds employment. We need to encourage our scientists; we need to develop a thorough-going policy in space research. In the United States for some time now there has been a full fledged congressional committee devoted primarily to space research. In the United Kingdom they had a minister who was responsible for this same area of space research.
I think it is time to see what is going on, and not just at the level of the civil service. I know we have in the civil service a number of people who are very competent in this field. I think it is time the representatives of the people had an opportunity to sit down and ask what are the facts, what are the capabilities of our country in the field of space research, and what are the kind of

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion things we might be doing. We might complement the facilities developed in the United States. Money is not the main obstacle in terms of space research. It is ideas, far-sighted and well designed policy. I would hope the government would see it in their power when we come back after the recess this fall, if there is going to be a recess, to have appointed immediately a special parliamentary committee which will do more than examine the many possibilities which are before us.
Let me quote in conclusion three or four suggestions made by an outspoken man, a space engineer, Dr. Gerald V. Bull:
An arctic radio television satellite system that would provide reliable reception in the far north.
How important this would be in respect of northern communications.
A navigation satellite that could determine precisely the geography and mineralogy of the country.
That would be quite an improvement. There are a number of other suggestions all of which could be within the competence and financial resources of this country. I am most anxious to hear the views of the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) in this regard because I feel we can look forward to great and enlightened things from him. I would hope that we can begin to look for an exciting and important policy in space research for this country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I commend the hon. member for his interest in and enthusiasm for space research, which he has described as a new frontier. While there would be those who would argue that Canada still has frontiers of a terrestrial character, I do think there is effort to spare and that certainly the time has come for us to look beyond the terrestrial limits. There is no doubt that in North America, and this is going over into Canada, there is a great interest in space research.
The hon. member has suggested the formation of a parliamentary committee to seek the answers to a number of questions concerning what we are doing, what we can do, what possibilities are open to us and how we can fit in with the programs of other nations, and perhaps make use of our talents. I should like to say that in my view, before this kind of program can be effectively tackled by a parliamentary committee, it is necessary to assemble the facts and to get some valid scientific views, particularly on future possibilities.
July 5. 1966

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion [DOT] (10:40 p.m.)
To this end the science secretariat of the Privy Council office early this spring commissioned a full scale study and review of what is being done in respect of space research in Canada, not only by the various government departments but also by universities, and an assessment of future areas in which we might be more active than we have been in the past. There is no question but that space research is a costly operation. With the limited resources of a country such as Canada we cannot attempt a complete space program on our own. We must do it in co-operation with others, and in those specialized fields to which our particular talents lend themselves.

It is my hope that this study will be presented to the Science Council not later than December of this year. When we are in the position to get the views of the Science Council, whose object the house will recall is precisely to lay out general guide lines for scientific research activities for the whole of Canada in the future, and when we have had the benefit of a review and an assessment exposed to the Science Council, I think it would be extremely useful for a parliamentary committee to look at the situation and give the necessary enthusiasm and impetus to this whole field.
